articles.title: Presidential villa suffers water and power cuts, Nigerian leader says
articles.summary: Bola Tinubu says he was shaving last week when the water cut out - an experience familiar to many Nigerians.
body: Bola Tinubu promised to address the country's electricity problems while campaigning for the 2023 election
Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu says the presidential villa suffers from cuts in electricity and water - issues that are all too common for the country's ordinary citizens.
He said he was shaving last week when the water supply cut at the villa, known as Aso Rock, in Abuja.
He is seeking re-election next January and vowed to address these issues.
Tinubu made the disclosure on Sunday at a special prayer session organised in his honour by members of his family in Lagos.
He explained: "On the Wednesday of last week, I was shaving, and the water went off. In the villa, you won't know punishment dey dia too [there’s punishment there too in Nigerian pidgin].
"The water went off. So we will correct all this. No light, no water, no electricity, no development. We have just started. We can do it, and we will do it for Nigeria,” he said.
Aso Villa serves as both the office and official residence of the Nigerian president. It is situated at the base of Aso Rock in Abuja.
Can Nigeria's president regain voters' trust after painful first term?
Search and rescue teams race against time after Nigeria boat tragedy

Nigeria has long endured electricity shortages, but recent severe disruptions have been caused primarily by insufficient gas supplies and declining hydropower output, rather than the usual nationwide grid collapse.
Persistent blackouts in Lagos, Abuja and elsewhere have forced distribution companies to implement rotating power cuts, severely impacting households and businesses.

The country also suffers from chronic water shortages, the result of a structural crisis rooted in the gap between rapid urban population growth and decaying, inadequate public water infrastructure, leaving millions without reliable supplies, especially in Lagos.
Many Nigerians rely on generators like these to power their homes and businesses

Tinubu made a high-profile electricity promise during the 2023 election campaign, but the exact wording and how binding it is has become a major point of contention ahead of the election on 16 January 2027.

In 2022, months before the last presidential election, Tinubu said: "Whichever way, by all means necessary, you will have electricity, and you will not pay for estimated bills any more. A promise made will be a promise kept.
"If I don't keep the promise and I come for a second term, don't vote for me, unless I give you adequate reasons why I couldn't deliver,” he said.

Despite the continuing power cuts, some of his supporters point to improved electricity supplies in rural areas as well as a recently approved $2bn (£1.5bn) investment in a new East–West Super Grid, designed to expand electricity transmission capacity and strengthen the national grid, as evidence that he is doing his best to keep to his promise.
Tinubu defeated the country’s former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar as well as former Anambra state governor Peter Obi in 2023 and the three are seen as the strongest contenders once again.

articles.title: Boy, 7, pulled alive from rubble hours after Russian strike on Ukraine, rescuers say
articles.summary: Nine people are dead in the attack, with rescue efforts ongoing to find those still missing from the residential building.
body: 'Danger seems greater all the time': Ukrainians search for missing after Russian strikes hit Kyiv

A seven-year-old boy has been rescued from the rubble of a residential building in Dymer after 14 hours, in overnight Russian strikes on Dymer, in the Kyiv region, that killed nine people, Ukrainian officials have said.
The attack occurred in the early hours of Sunday. A 79-year-old woman was also rescued alive from the collapsed building, Kyiv's regional head Tymur Tkachenko said.
A strike on a private home in Bila Tserkva killed one more person and set the building ablaze, he added.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also said three people were killed and 13 wounded in a separate strike on Vyshneve, also in the Kyiv region, that hit a grocery store on Sunday.
Ukrainian authorities said the boy in Dymer is in stable condition and was taken to hospital, and have thanked everyone involved in saving his life.
Zelensky and Ukraine's national police also confirmed the rescue of the boy.
Response teams including police, explosive technicians, dog handlers and medics are continuing with rescue efforts.
In a telegram post, Tkachenko said the 79-year-old woman rescued from the rubble was receiving treatment in hospital.
Earlier he said six people were injured in the attack, while others were still missing.
The attack on the residential building occurred in the early hours of the morning while people were asleep
Zelensky said more than 130 people are involved in emergency operations at the scene, and that they will continue until they have "complete information about every single person".
Sending his condolences to the families and loved ones of those killed, he said the strike struck the residential building, "practically blowing a section of it to smithereens".
Zelensky added that "rescue efforts are complicated by constant new air raid alerts and renewed threats".
The strike hit the building at 05:00 local time, when families were still asleep, Ukraine's minister of internal affairs Ivan Vyhivskyi said.
More than 70 strikes have been launched across 10 Ukrainian regions as of Sunday evening, Vyhivskyi added.
Emergency workers continue to search for those missing after Russian drone and missile attacks in Dymer.
In his video address posted online, Zelensky also said three people were killed and 13 injured in a strike on an "ordinary grocery store" in Vyshneve.
Tkachenko previously said two other people were killed and eight wounded in the Vyshneve attack.
Russia also struck a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Ukraine's Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said in a post on X., external

articles.title: South Korea education minister resigns over exam cheating scandal
articles.summary: Choi Kyo-jin admits last-minute measures to stop AI-assisted cheating during the college entrance exam caused chaos.
body: How South Korea tackles cheating on its college entrance exam
South Korea's Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin has resigned over an exam cheating scandal that shocked the nation.
He said he took full responsibility for the confusion caused by last-minute measures aimed at stopping AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's annual college entrance exam, known as Suneung.

A week ago, the top scorer in the national tax accountancy exam admitted using a mini-camera, mobile phone and AI tools. This prompted officials to act urgently to detect hidden devices, including sending emergency alerts to every single mobile phone in the country.
The Suneung takes up to nine hours to complete, and it plays a big role in career trajectories of millions of South Koreans.
South Korean high school pupils in Daegu check their answers, a day after the annual college entrance exam
"As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi was quoted as saying on Sunday by South Korea's Yonhap's news agency.
"Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation," the minister added.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung - who has been calling for an overhaul of the current exam system - later accepted Choi's resignation.
The education ministry earlier said 111 candidates had been found with unauthorised smart devices during this year's Suneung, which was taken by about 500,000 students.
Concerns over academic dishonesty during the fiercely competitive exam had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.
These fears came to a boil last weekend, when Han Won-seok, the top tax accountancy exam scorer in April, admitted to cheating.
His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong.
"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI, then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating," the 34-year-old said in a video message.
This prompted the authorities to introduce urgent measures, with just days ahead of the Suneung.
This included sending nationwide emergency alerts on the exam day.

Three alerts were sent between 08:00 and 15:00 local time on Thursday, causing phones across the country to blare out in unison - even if they were on silent mode, and even if they belonged to tourists using data roaming.
The phones did not ring out if they were switched off or on airplane mode.
It was the first time that South Korea used its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters.
Candidates also had to cover up the buttons on their shirts and jackets to block any hidden cameras, and authorities conducted inspections of eyewear.
All this made even honest test takers paranoid.
Ahead of the Suneung, one high school senior told the Korea Times he was worried his horn-rimmed spectacles would be mistaken for smart glasses.
Another told Yonhap he usually wore glasses but made an effort to put on contact lenses for the Suneung to avoid raising suspicions.

articles.title: Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 after flipping North Carolina seat
articles.summary: Democrats have now won at least 258 seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats.
body: Chuck Hubbard is a former journalist whose first political campaign was in 2022
The Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina.
The race was called on Sunday, with Hubbard beating Foxx by 330 votes with 99% counted. It was one of the closest contests of the recent midterm elections, in which Democrats also secured the Senate.
The party has now won at least 258 House seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats, with four races still yet to be called.
Neither party had won as many House races since 1992, when Bill Clinton won the presidency and Democrats won a total of 258 seats.
View the 2026 midterm election results

Sunday's result came after Foxx, who has represented North Carolina's 5th Congressional District since 2005, requested a recount. This is allowed under state law when the margin of victory is under 1%.

She conceded on Sunday, saying in a statement: "After running a campaign focused on my track record of commonsense solutions and conservative values, I'm humbled and grateful that so many North Carolina voters responded by supporting my candidacy, even if we came up just a few votes short."
Virginia Foxx spent a decade in the North Carolina Senate before representing the state in the House of Representatives
Hubbard, meanwhile, wrote on X that he had spoken to Foxx, "who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process".

He added: "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District."

Hubbard's win, which comes after he lost to Foxx in the 2024 midterms by nine percentage points, followed a number of Democratic victories in deeply Republican districts including South Carolina, Texas, Alaska and Iowa.
Hubbard, like many Democrats running in the midterms, focused on the rising cost of living in the US during the war with Iran - a top issue for voters.
President Donald Trump himself - as well as Vice President JD Vance - have suggested inflation caused by the war in Iran was probably to blame for the Republican losses.
Hubbard has also said he will also prioritise working families and small businesses, supporting public education and expanding access to affordable healthcare, according to his website.

The remaining House races yet to be called are in Tennessee and Minnesota, while two elections in Louisiana will go to a runoff in December. In Tennessee's fourth district, Democrat Victoria Broderick leads by fewer than 300 votes, and in Minnesota's first district, Democrat Jake Johnson is winning by fewer than 500 votes.

Democrats may use their upcoming majority in the House and control of the Senate to investigate conflicts of interest and other actions by the president and those close to him, while the Senate also has the power to confirm or block the president's cabinet and judicial nominations. They will also be able to pass legislation through Congress easily, though Trump still has to give final sign off for it to become law.
However, even with control of both chambers of Congress, they will still have limits on their power as Trump can veto legislation.

articles.title: Russia-bound ship attacked in Gulf of Finland
articles.summary: Finnish defence forces say that Ukraine was likely behind the drone attack on the vessel.
body: The Finnish Border Guard is leading the operations involving the Sparta II
A Russian cargo vessel bound for the country's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad has been hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, Russian and Finnish authorities say.

The ship - the Sparta II - caught on fire after the strike on Saturday morning, before drifting into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones had been used, based on preliminary information, and there was "no threat" to the territory's supplies.
The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.
The company says on its website that it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.

Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.
This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.
Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".

A Russian rescue vessel approached the ship and was told by the crew that they did not need to be evacuated, Kaliningrad's governor wrote on Telegram, adding: "The crew is currently carrying out the necessary work and plans to continue on its way."

The Finnish Border Guard later said the crew had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was now already en route to Russia. The Russian rescue vessel had remained at the location of the stricken ship.
It added that no environmental damage had been detected and that there was no danger to maritime traffic or people.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.
Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said that the Finnish Border Guard were responsible for the investigation into the attack and were co-operating with other relevant authorities.
Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.

The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.
Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland.

articles.title: US Army to detonate tonnes of unstable explosives in Iowa despite court order
articles.summary: The Army says "swift action" is necessary to protect its personnel and nearby communities around its ammunition plant in Iowa.
body: The US Army plans to move ahead with detonating five tonnes of degraded explosives in Iowa despite a ruling to halt it indefinitely, a new court filing shows.

"To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action," the justice department notified the court on Saturday. "Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay."
The court had ordered a pause after environmental groups sued to stop the detonation, arguing the army failed to consider safer alternatives.
The detonation was originally scheduled for Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. The army now plans to act by 24 November under an emergency exemption.

In the new filing, the Department of the Army argued that a controlled detonation was necessary to protect the public from an unplanned explosion, a risk it said would become more likely as temperatures were set to fall in the coming days.

"There is an immediate risk that the lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant will explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1C) in the next several days," the filing states.
It argued that the army had removed the doors to the bunker where the barrels were stored in preparation for the detonation and that made the explosives more "vulnerable to temperature changes".
The government has not released details for the rescheduled detonation.

Earlier, the army had warned residents to leave their homes for six hours on the original scheduled day of the explosion, for the duration of the explosion and until the dust settled. An advisory warned "all humans" to avoid being outside in the affected areas while the demolition detonation was set to take place.

Lead azide is a highly volatile compound used as a detonator. Earlier this year, the IAAAP found that the material had degraded over time to the point where it was now too risky to move the material, according to Iowa Public Radio.
On Friday, the military said it was working with the Department of Health and Human Services and the EPA to ensure the explosion was done in the safest manner possible.
Military and environmental officials determined that detonating it in place was the safest way to eliminate the explosive safety hazard.

The EPA, which granted an emergency permit to detonate 68 drums of the material, said it did so because the explosion risk "presented an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment".

One of the Environmental groups suing to pause the detonation, the Iowa Environmental Council, argued that many Iowans living within the risk-zone were unaware that the explosion was scheduled to happen.
"There is no safe level of lead exposure, and Iowans were given just days to prepare for the November 20 detonation," the organisation said in a press statement.
The Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club, which filed the lawsuit on Thursday that prompted the court-ordered pause, filed a new motion on Sunday in response to the army's filing.
The group asks the court to pause proceedings so that it may submit additional information before the scheduled detonation.

The motion includes declarations from environmental experts and local officials who support pausing the detonation, citing a lack of public notice and questioning the Army's claim that delay would cause significant risks.

articles.title: Three killed and dozens missing after fire at Indonesian factory
articles.summary: At least three people were killed and 36 are still missing after a fire at a confectionary factory.
body: At least three people have been killed and 36 are still missing after a fire at a confectionary factory in western Java on Saturday.
Firefighters were still tackling some flames on Sunday, while rescuers searched for the missing in parts of the damaged building where workers were believed to be trapped.
Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency said on Sunday 15 survivors had been located, and four others taken to hospital and a local clinic with undisclosed injuries.
The factory is in Serang district, Banten province, about 50km (31km) west of Jakarta. Authorities have not yet determined the fire's cause.
Banten Governor, Andra Soni, told media about 60 people were believed to be inside the factory when it caught fire on Saturday evening.

Photos and footage of the scene showed the large factory taken over by flames during the night, firefighters battling the flames, and first responders retrieving at least one body from the wreckage on Sunday morning.
"All members of the joint SAR team are making every effort to locate the missing victims while prioritising the safety of personnel on the ground," the rescue agency said.
Relatives of the missing workers had gathered outside the factory waiting for updates, according to local broadcasts cited by AFP.

Firefighters had been called to the building at 16:30 local time (09:30 GMT) on Saturday - but it was already engulfed in flames, broadcaster Kompas TV reported, citing fire official Tubugas Machfudz.
"When we arrived (on location)... a large area was already on fire. So we could not determine whether the company's protection system was functioning properly or not," he said.
The factory is owned by PT Fonusa Agung Mulia, according to search and rescue authorities.
On LinkedIn the company describes itself as a subsidiary of UNIFAM, one of Indonesia's largest food and beverage companies.

articles.title: Mexican drug lord on FBI's 10 most wanted list arrested in shoot-out
articles.summary: Fausto Isidro "Chapo Idisro" Meza Flores, who is accused of drug trafficking and torture, is detained after gun fight with authorities.
body: Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores was detained by Mexican special forces on Friday
A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities.
Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores was detained along with his lieutenant by Mexican special forces in Guasave, Sinaloa on Friday, Mexico's defence secretariat said.

Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organised crime charges, while he has been accused of "flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and other deadly drugs" by the FBI. The US is seeking his extradition.
Mexico has stepped up efforts to tackle drug-related crime after coming under pressure from US President Donald Trump since he returned to the White House.

Meza Flores, the leader of the Meza Flores Organisation, also known as the Guasave Cartel, is thought to have been active in the drug trafficking trade since the 1990s but managed to evade authorities till now by maintaining a relatively low profile.

Using US intelligence on his whereabouts, Mexican special forces descended on his location using "stealth and surprise", establishing a perimeter to prevent him from escaping and reinforcements arriving, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
However, they "came under attack from gunfire and explosives" before entering the property and arresting Meza Flores and his second-in-command, it added.
Videos circulating online appear to show helicopters firing streams of bullets towards the ground in Guasave. Others appear to show people at a baseball stadium fleeing as they hear shooting sounds.
A number of vehicles were pictured burning on a highway near Los Mochis, Sinaloa, after Fausto Isidro "Chapo Idisro" Meza Flores was arrested
The two detainees were subsequently flown to Mexico City to face prosecution, the defence secretariat said.
When he was added to the FBI's most-wanted list in 2025, he was accused of "heinous crimes" including kidnapping, extortion and torture.
Then-acting FBI director Brian Driscoll said Meza Flores and his organisation had also unleashed a "scourge of illicit drugs" into the US via its southern border with Mexico.
He was initially charged with drug trafficking in the US in 2012 before being charged again in 2019.
The 44-year-old is alleged to have conspired to manufacture and distribute large quantities of cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and marijuana between 2005 and 2019.
Meza Flores was originally a high-ranking member of the Beltrán Leyva Organization, but a split between rival factions led to a surge of violence and prompted him to establish his own cartel by 2013.

His organisation has also engaged in what US officials described as an "extremely violent turf war" with the Sinaloa Cartel, one of the most powerful drug trafficking gangs, which operates in the same region.
Meza Flores was added to the FBI's most-wanted list after Mexican authorities reportedly linked his cartel to 20 million fentanyl pills they seized in 2024.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has taken a tougher stance on the country's cartels in a bid to resist US intervention on Mexican soil. Mexico has welcomed closer collaboration but resisted US boots on the ground.
Trump made stemming the flow of drugs into the US across its southern border one of his key election pledges.

articles.title: Italian jeweller and businessman Paolo Bulgari dies aged 89
articles.summary: In a statement to Italian media, his family remember him as "the greatest jeweller of our time".
body: Italian jeweller Paolo Bulgari, who helped turn his family's business into a global luxury brand, has died in Rome aged age 89.
His family announced the news, remembering him as "the greatest jeweller of our time", according to Italian media.
Paolo Bulgari was Chairman of the Bvlgari Group since 1984 and its jewellery pieces have adorned Hollywood stars and royalty including Diana, Princess of Wales.
The company Bvlgari posted an online tribute to the "true creative soul", whose work would "continue to inspire generations to come".
The firm, Bulgari, was set up by his grandfather, Greek silversmith Sotirios Voulgaris, in Rome in the late 19th century - who later adapted his name to Bulgari in Italian.

Originally from Paramythia, a mountain village in the Epirus region of northwestern Greece renowned for its silver jewellery, Voulgaris fled Ottoman rule and settled in Naples before opening a shop in Rome.
Paolo Bulgari joined the company shortly after leaving school, becoming an expert in gemstones - eventually leading the business and overseeing international growth.

The Bulgari family favoured bold gemstones, rich yellow gold, generous proportions and unexpected colour combinations to set them apart from the delicate asethetic associated with Parisian jewellery houses.
The business broke into luxury markets and diversified beyond jewellery into watches, perfumes, leather goods and hotels.

"Paolo Bulgari began collaborating with his father in 1960, specialising in the knowledge of precious stones, of which he was one of the world's leading experts, and refining the sensibility and aesthetic sense that are at the root of the Bvlgari style," the Bvlgari company posted on social media., external
"He poured his heart into his craft and into nurturing the talents of young designers, leaving an indelible mark on the world of jewellery.
"Thank you, Mr. Paolo, your legacy as a brilliant beacon of creative inspiration will continue to inspire generations to come."
Paolo Bulgari alongside David Bowie and his wife Iman in September 1991 in Versailles, France.
The post included a quote from Paolo Bulgari: "Everything can be a source of inspiration. There are no rules in creativity. Never."
The designer brand's celebrity clients have included Elizabeth Taylor, Audrey Hepburn, Marilyn Monroe, Ingrid Bergman, Sophie Loren, Anne Hathaway, Zendaya and Rihanna.
Actor Zendaya wearing a Bvlgari necklace at the 2025 Golden Globe awards.
In 2011 the family sold its controlling stake to the French luxury group LVMH, in a deal worth about 3.7 billion euros.
In 2019, he and his wife established the Paolo Bulgari Foundation to support young people through schooling and job training in disadvantaged neighbourhoods on the outskirts of Rome.
The funeral will take place in Rome on Monday, 23 November in the Basilica of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme.
LVMH to take over Italy's Bulgari

articles.title: FBI reportedly investigating apparent hack of its criminal database
articles.summary: The National Crime Information Center database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information.
body: The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its criminal information database, US media reports, citing two people briefed on the issue.
The National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information on warrants and background checks. The BBC contacted the FBI for comment.

This comes after a string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors in the US last week. Officials have said they were not caused by cyberattacks, but the blackouts have sparked scrutiny from lawmakers.
White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired this week, with US President Donald Trump saying he was not good enough.
It would not be the first time hackers have targeted the FBI, the domestic intelligence and security service of the US.
In September, the FBI said it was investigating an apparent breach by a cyber-crime group ShinyHunters, which claimed it had stolen sensitive information on all bureau staff - around 38,000 people.

After that hack, one former FBI agent told the BBC he feared for the safety of current employees, whose personal information could soon become available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers.
In a separate development, NBC reported an apparent cyberattack against the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) .
Employees were informed on Thursday that its farm payment system had been targeted, NBC said.
The USDA has not publicly commented on the issue.

articles.title: Lock of former US President George Washington's hair sells for $4,000
articles.summary: The hair was given as a sign of friendship shortly before Washington's death in 1799, according to a descendent of its former owner.
body: George Washington died in 1799 after serving for two terms as America's first president
A framed lock of hair from America's first president, George Washington, has been sold at auction for $4,000 (£3,058).

The hair once belonged to John Gadsby, who entertained Washington in 1799 just before the latter's death the same year, and was later obtained by a collector called John K Lattimer from a descendent of Gadsby's, according to Richmond Auctions, which sold the item.
Its new owner has not been named.

Saturday's sale is not the most expensive for Washington hair at auction. Three strands thought to have been removed from him close to or after his death stored in a locket sold for nearly $40,000 in 2021.

Gadsby, a resident of what in 1799 was the town of Alexandria in Virginia, entertained Washington for dinner shortly before his death later that year, according to a testament given in 1928 by Gadsby's granddaughter, Julia Ten Eyck McBlair, and which was posted on the Richmond Auctions website.

McBlair stated that her grandfather came into possession of Washington's hair "in view of the friendship and association with his last days" and had it framed and hung "under General Washington's portrait in our home in Washington City, there I have seen it all my life".
Gadsby hosted Washington's two birthday celebrations in 1798 and 1799, Richmond Auctions states.

Washington led American forces to victory against the British in the War of Independence and helped draft the US Constitution before becoming the country's first president in 1788. He stepped down in 1797 after serving two terms.
Several locks of Washington's hair have been preserved, including at least 50 examples that are in a collection at his former residence, Mount Vernon, which is now a museum.
"Public displays of hair from friends or loved ones peaked in the 19th century, but had long been popular among affluent families like the Washingtons," a blog on the Mount Vernon website states.
As well as lockets of his hair, other items associated with Washington have also done well at auction.
In July, a signed letter by Washington from 1776, in which he asks for soldiers for the Continental Army to fight the British, sold for $109,800.

articles.title: Natural beauty made this New Zealand tourist village. Now it threatens its existence
articles.summary: Famed for its nearby glacier, Franz Josef village faces ‘catastrophic’ flooding and deaths if action not taken to manage the Waiho River
body: The small village of Franz Josef sits on the rugged west coast of New Zealand’s South Island, its natural beauty providing the drawcard for a million tourists to pack its hotels, spas and restaurants every year.

But that drawcard – which has turned it into a hotspot for everything from hiking to kayaking and made it one of the country’s most popular destinations – may change the course of the village’s fate once again.
Its collection of buildings lies in the shadow of the famed Franz Josef glacier, on an alpine fault and beside the Waiho River, a globally rare braided river. And the river is rising.
Related: ‘Slipping through our fingers’: New Zealand scientists distraught at scale of glacier loss

The latest technical report, released in September, shows the Waiho is rapidly rising and changing course – several years earlier than previously predicted – and scientists warn that Franz Josef is at risk of “catastrophic” flooding and deaths if action is not taken to release its waters. The report shows the original 10-year plan to release water from the river needs to be brought forward.

“If the full force of the Waiho goes through the township, then the structures, buildings – whatever is in its way – will be significantly damaged, if not destroyed,” says Prof Ian Fuller, a fluvial geomorphologist and spokesperson for the independent Waiho technical advisory group, set up to advise the West Coast regional council.
“We’ve now got seven years ... essentially we need to be doing 10 years work in seven,” Fuller said.
Since the report’s release, scientists have been calling for urgent intervention to prevent a disaster, which has prompted local authorities to accelerate their river management plans.
While links to climate change affecting the river are tenuous at this stage, global warming and El Niño will bring more rainfall and the potential of floods, Fuller says.

Adding to the risk, there is a 75% probability of a magnitude eight earthquake within the next 50 years, according to Earth Sciences NZ. A rupture could trigger flooding, landslides and cause “wholesale destruction of the town,” Fuller says, describing the damage as “potentially catastrophic”.

But he was quick to reassure residents they could “sleep safely in their beds” because the river and rainfall are closely monitored, while urging better evacuation plans and information signs for tourists.The community is not living with fear, says Janelle Shaw, a Franz Josef resident and chair of the Glacier Country Tourism Group. But it is becoming increasingly frustrated at the lack of action. “We’re three years on from when a similar report was released, and we have made no further progress.”
Related: Many of New Zealand’s glaciers could disappear in a decade, scientists warn
For years, Shaw, alongside the residents and community association, has lobbied authorities to include the community in its planning.

“It has to be something that’s happening with the community rather than something that’s happening to the community,” she said, adding the Westland District Council’s new working group, which is supposed to include residents, is a good first step.

Braided rivers move large amounts of gravel and sediment downstream, but in narrowed rivers, the gravel builds upwards, instead of spreading out. The Waiho riverbed is rising about 20 centimetres a year. A large amount of sediment accumulating near the glacier could accelerate the problem if a storm pushes it downstream.

Since the 1980s, stopbanks – a long mound of gravel and soil that limits water spreading on to land – have been erected to contain the river, to make way for land-use such as building, farming and infrastructure. The rising riverbed makes stopbanks more vulnerable to flooding.
“Now the bed of the river is perched two metres above the land adjacent to the river, in the vicinity of the township,” Fuller says.

In 2023, the advisory group found the river was carving out a new channel, north of Franz Josef village. It recommended a 10-year plan to give the river room to move and lessen flood risk. But in September, the group found the river is changing much faster than initially predicted, despite a period of relatively quiet weather.

Franz Josef has long discussed the possibility of relocating the village, but the advisory group recommends first releasing the river’s southern stopbanks to allow the water to fan out and slow the rate of riverbed rise.
It would buy the village time, but requires relocating the highway, wastewater infrastructure and landfills, and submerging swathes of private farmland at a cost of more than $200m (£83m).
Westland District’s mayor, Helen Lash, says the prospect of releasing the river is “very raw” for the community.

“These homes and farms are where they live, what they have invested in and brought their families up in,” Lash says. “It’s a damn hard conversation to have with anyone but it is something we have to look at … if we are to protect the northern side of the town.”
Lash has formed a working group in response to the report, with relevant agencies, local authorities and the community aiming to present a plan to the government in early 2027.

A future government – which will be confirmed when the country’s election results are finalised on 27 November – will decide how to manage the situation. Simon Watts, the minister for local government and climate change, has said authorities are working on legislation to ensure councils are creating adaptation plans for areas exposed to natural hazards.
But Fuller is concerned the government is not acting with enough urgency and pointed to January’s deadly landslide in Tauranga – a known hazard before disaster struck – as a warning.
“We cannot allow that to happen at Franz Josef,” he says. “We know about the risk. We’ve got a solution. It requires investment. There’s no need for anyone to lose life here.”

articles.title: Butt of the joke: Trump impersonator mocks president at Canada press dinner
articles.summary: Carney watches on as comedian lampoons US leader and his interest in men’s backsides at correspondents’ event Ottawa
body: Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, was joined on stage in Ottawa by a Donald Trump impersonator who mocked the US president to raucous laughter from a crowd of politicians and journalists at a parliamentary press gallery dinner on Saturday.

With coiffed hair and an ill-fitting suit, comedian Mark Critch – who portrays the president on the sketch show This Hour Has 22 Minutes – danced on to the stage and lampooned the trade war Trump started as well as the president’s threats to annex Canada.
“We’re going to have a great deal,” Critch said, channeling Trump’s distinct mannerisms. “There’s only one thing standing in the way: me, because I’m crazy.”
The fake Trump continued that he was “so popular we just had a big, blue wave”, a reference to the Democratic rout of Republicans in this month’s US midterm elections.

He also mocked Trump’s frequent mentions of other men’s physiques, saying of the comedian Mark McKinney, who was portraying Carney, that he had “a great ass – doesn’t he? What a beautiful ass, he’s got such an incredible ass.”
Related: Trump forced to play good sport at correspondents’ dinner – but it couldn’t last

He earned the most laughter of his short appearance for saying of Carney: “I don’t call him the governor to his face, because I’m a coward”. The real Trump has frequently attempted to insult Canada’s leaders by calling them governor, not prime minister, suggesting Canada is a US state.
The annual dinner, attended by media, political leaders and lobbyists, is often defined by carefully written jokes by the staff of party leaders.
Throughout his own 16-minute set, Carney poked fun at his political rivals, the media and the US president.
At one point, he remarked: “Damn, this is a tough room, and I’ve been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator.”
Clips of the dinner, including the crowd laughing at the president, have circulated widely on US media.
The newly appointed governor general, Louise Arbour, also gave a speech, including a nod to the prime minister’s decision to travel extensively around the globe.

“Our prime minister is already getting a lot of attention. Actually, I heard a guy the other day compare him to God. Now seriously, do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney? God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he’s supposed to be,” she said.
The Conservative leader, Pierre Poilievre, also used the evening to poke fun at his own reputation.

“Some say that Mark has a controlling leadership style. There’s been reports that he yells and micromanages his staff. He acts like a miserable prick to journalists,” he said. “And when I hear things like that, I say once again, he’s stealing all my ideas.”

He attracted a stunned silence, however, for alluding to Justin Trudeau’s relationship with Katy Perry, saying, “Trudeau is running around the world doing to a faded pop princess what he did to Canada” while prime minister, a remark that was widely criticised as demeaning to the pop star.

The New Democratic party leader, Avi Lewis, who has not yet won a seat in parliament, took a shot at Carney’s early exit from the event, as well his own party’s dismal standings. “I do not have a seat in the House of Commons, but when I am given one at dinner, I stay there all night long,” he said.

articles.title: Israel seeks to jail Palestinian student activist without trial after dorm arrest
articles.summary: Mahdi Tounsi appeared with visible bruising after being interrogated by police on his association with Israeli-Palestinian organisations
body: Israeli professors, students and rights activists are calling for the immediate release of Mahdi Tounsi, a sociology student at Jerusalem’s Hebrew University who has been held without charge for more than two weeks after he was seized from his dorm room.

The detention comes amid a racist campaign of delegitimisation against Palestinian citizens of Israel, whose votes were critical to stripping Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition of its majority in elections last month.
Police took Tounsi, 26, a criminology and sociology student from East Jerusalem who is active in Jewish-Palestinian campaign groups, from his dorm room on 8 November.
When he appeared by video link at a court hearing on 19 November he had visible bruises on his face, did not have the glasses he needs to see properly, and his hair and beard had been shaved.

Tounsi told his lawyer that police beat him in the dorm, in the patrol car and at the police station, Israeli media reported. Interrogators questioned him about his activism with Israeli-Palestinian organisations Standing Together and Ir Amim.
Both groups called for his immediate release and warned against using security agencies to silence political activity and critical speech.

“[This] could happen to any student and any one of us, especially in a month when the government is persecuting Arab citizens, from [journalist] Abed Abu Shehadeh to the leaders of Arab political parties,” Standing Together said in a statement, calling on the university to intervene to ensure a fair judicial process.

Ir Amim described Tounsi as thoughtful, gentle and a valued partner “in movements bringing Palestinians and Israelis together”, in a statement that also warned of “serious concerns for his safety, wellbeing, and right to due process”.

After losing the election, Netanyahu and his allies weaponised false accusations of mass fraud – Israel’s election commission validated the results – in an attempt to hold on to power by delegitimising the votes of Palestinian citizens of Israel.
The prime minister has also been accused of politicising security institutions in his campaign against Palestinian-led parties, and fostering a rise in racist rhetoric.

When police powers to hold Tounsi under the original arrest warrant expired last week, they submitted an order to hold him without trial in administrative detention, signed by the defence minister, Israel Katz.

The administrative detention law allows Israel to hold individuals for up to six months without charging them or allowing them to see evidence against them, although it has to be presented in a closed court.
Because the Shin Bet security force did not send a representative to the hearing on Tounsi’s detention last week, it was postponed until Tuesday.

Ahead of the court hearing, Jewish and Palestinian students demonstrated at universities across the country, including Jerusalem and Tel Aviv, with signs including “Free Mahdi” and “Kidnapping Palestinians will not silence justice”.
The university authorities did not inform his family, and his detention only came to light after concerned friends reported him missing.

Hebrew University said in a statement that it was notified about the arrest shortly before police seized Tounsi, that no university representatives were present when he was detained and police afterwards said the arrest took place “without unusual incidents”.
It did not directly address the allegations of police violence, his visible bruising, the shaving of his head and beard, removal of his glasses or the shifting legal framework.

“The university is not a party to the legal proceedings involving the student, and we do not have information that would allow us to comment on the circumstances leading to the arrest or on the ongoing legal proceedings,” the statement said.
“We are concerned for his wellbeing,” the statement added, saying the university hoped “that his rights will be fully respected throughout the process”.
Israeli police did not respond to requests for comment about Tounsi’s detention.

Tounsi is a resident of East Jerusalem, not a Palestinian citizen of Israel. Palestinians holding that status can move freely inside Israel and Jerusalem but are stateless and can not vote in Israeli national elections.

articles.title: If Trump, Xi and Putin are carving up the pudding, who gets the sixpence?
articles.summary: Letters: Readers respond to an article by Rafael Behr on the Shenzhen summit, where the three world leaders met without a place at the table for Europe
body: Rafael Behr (Trump, Xi and Putin have a shared vision of global power – with no place for Europe, 18 November) draws parallels between the Shenzhen summit and Winston Churchill, Joseph Stalin and Franklin D Roosevelt meeting at Yalta. I see it as bringing us a step closer to George Orwell’s Nineteen Eighty-Four, in which the world is divided into three superstates: Oceania, Eurasia and Eastasia.

We already have the surveillance in the form of CCTV, facial-recognition technology and email trawling. Daily we witness the rewriting of history. We could be sleepwalking into a situation from which we will be unable to escape.Andy FazakerleyIrby, Wirral

• Rafael Behr says: “The image of three leaders calibrating the balance of global power has been compared to Yalta, February 1945”. In the absence of Ukrainians, a more accurate comparison would be Munich, September 1938, where the fate of Czechoslovakia was decided without Czech participation.Peter DavisWelwyn, Hertfordshire

• I cannot be the only one who, on seeing the pictures of Xi, Putin and Trump meeting in Shenzhen, thought of James Gillray’s 1805 cartoon The Plumb-pudding in Danger, depicting William Pitt the Younger and Napoleon Bonaparte carving up the globe between them. I wonder who will end up with the silver sixpence?Catherine RoseOlney, Buckinghamshire

• Trump, Xi and Putin’s summit’s group photo makes me despair. This has been an attempt to give credibility to Putin and Trump’s warmongering. How dare they have the audacity to make a “joint peace declaration”. As my mother used to say when seeing shady people, “Would you trust them to take you across the road”?Chris WaltersBuxton, Derbyshire
